posts.text: If your wallet is small and it’s still not growing, read this. You don’t need bigger trades. You need better risk management. Let’s say you have a $200 wallet. Before entering any trade, decide one thing first: “How much am I okay losing if this trade is wrong?” For example, fix your maximum risk at $5 per trade. Now don’t randomly put $5 as margin and choose 20x leverage. That’s not how it works. First find your entry, then find the technical stop-loss the level where your trade idea becomes invalid. Suppose your SL is 5% away. Maximum risk = $5 SL distance = 5% Position size = $5 ÷ 5% = $100 Only after this calculate the leverage according to the margin you want to use. If you use $10 margin: $100 ÷ $10 = 10x leverage So if the 5% SL gets hit, your planned loss is around $5, not your whole account. posts.text: Two Votes Instead of One Validators securing Ethereum (ETH) would eventually have to cast two separate votes instead of one under a draft improvement proposal that Ethereum researchers filed on Wednesday, October 21. Transactions slowed over the past 24 hours, and the ledger kept closing and validating throughout, only well behind its usual rhythm. posts.text: • Borderless.xyz's Q3 report put stablecoin remittance costs at a median $2 per $200 transfer • Traditional remittances cost $12.72 per $200, equal to 6.36% of the amount sent • Sub-Saharan Africa stablecoin transfers cost 2.9% versus 8.46% on traditional rails 84% Cheaper on a $200 Transfer Sending $200 across a border over stablecoin-funded payment rails costs a median of $2, against $12.72 through conventional channels in traditional finance, according to the third-quarter report from Borderless.xyz, a stablecoin payments network. Measured as a share of the amount sent, the report puts stablecoin rails at 1% and traditional transfers at 6.36%, which works out to roughly 84% in savings. Stablecoins, for readers new to the term, are blockchain-issued tokens pegged to a fiat currency, most commonly the US dollar, and cross-border payment has become one of their most active applications.

posts.text: On 21 October 2026, at slot 459,653,000, Solana switched its consensus engine. Finality—the moment a transaction becomes irreversible—moved from roughly 12.8 seconds under TowerBFT to a design target of about 150 milliseconds under the new protocol called Alpenglow. That single number is the entire story: a public blockchain now aims to settle in the same window that high-frequency trading desks and payment networks already treat as normal. Alpenglow is the largest consensus rewrite Solana has attempted since its 2020 launch. Built by Anza with research input from ETH Zurich, it replaces TowerBFT with a component called Votor. Votes no longer travel as on-chain transactions. Validators instead exchange lightweight BLS-signed messages that any node can aggregate into a compact certificate of roughly one kilobyte.
